column1: 1|After the new footbridge opened, cycling grew at an astonishing rate: the weekly count doubled within a month.|Use the two-word phrase for surprisingly rapid change: Membership increased at an ___ after the campaign.|a predictable slow rate|a rate that cannot change|Compare the size of the change with the short time available.|The doubling is presented as surprisingly rapid, not merely regular growth.

2|The library is increasingly busy: more readers arrive each week.|Use the adverb meaning to a growing degree: The evening classes became ___ popular over the year.|to a smaller degree|only on a single occasion|Follow the direction of the weekly trend.|The repeated rise in attendance makes this a growing degree of busyness.

4|The studio's expansion added two rooms to its original floor area.|Use the noun for becoming larger: The shop's ___ created space for another counter.|a reduction in size|a change of ownership only|Compare the space before and after the addition.|Adding rooms makes the studio larger; it does not just change who owns it.

5|An overground railway crosses the park on raised tracks rather than in a tunnel.|Write the two-word rail expression: Visitors can see the passing trains because the line is an ___.|railway operating only underground|a road used exclusively by buses|Locate the tracks relative to the ground.|The visible raised tracks identify the above-ground railway sense.

7|Extra delivery trips may result in heavier traffic near the market.|Use the two-word causal phrase: A missed connection can ___ a longer journey.|occur before without causing|provide an example of|Ask whether one event brings about another.|The note predicts a consequence of the extra trips rather than a simple sequence.

9|The ministry is based in the fictional country's capital, where its national government meets.|Use the city noun: The national parliament meets in the country's ___.|money available for investment|the largest city in every region|Keep the geographical meaning used by the government-location note.|The reference to the national government selects the main-city sense, not financial funds.

11|The guide calls the old assembly hall historic because a significant treaty was signed there.|Use the adjective for importance in history: The agreement was signed in a ___ building.|merely old with no stated significance|currently used for sports|The guide gives a reason the site matters to history.|The treaty supplies historical significance; age alone is not the point.

12|On the site plan, six garden paths form a ring around the pond.|Use the three-word phrase: The seats will ___ around the central display.|make a straight line|create separate unconnected corners|Imagine following the layout back to its starting point.|The paths surround the pond in a circular arrangement rather than crossing it in a line.

13|The welcome kit will consist of a map, a notebook and a pencil.|Use the two-word composition phrase: Each starter pack will ___ three small items.|be located beside|be delivered before|Focus on what belongs inside the whole set.|The listed objects are components of the kit, not nearby objects or delivery events.

14|The inspection described the shed as poorly built because its joints did not fit securely.|Use the two-word phrase for low construction quality: The report judged the shelter to be ___.|built with unusually high workmanship|constructed only very recently|The finding concerns workmanship rather than the building's age.|Loose-fitting joints support the judgment of low building quality.

16|The historical report used the word slum for an overcrowded district with very poor housing; the editor explains that the label must not define the residents.|Use the historical housing-area noun: The archive described the neglected district as a ___; the teacher will discuss the label's limitations.|a wealthy low-density residential area|a temporary queue at a station|Focus on the housing conditions described by the historical source, while treating residents respectfully.|The term refers to poor, crowded housing conditions; it is not a description of the worth of the people living there.

17|The museum label describes the cart as horse-drawn because two horses pulled it.|Use the hyphenated adjective: The display shows a ___ cart pulled by an animal.|powered by an electric battery|painted with pictures of horses|Identify the source of the pulling force.|The horses provide movement, so the adjective describes propulsion rather than decoration.

18|After three cancellations and a lost reservation, the traveller called the journey a nightmare.|Use the figurative noun for an extremely unpleasant experience: With delays and missing luggage, the trip became a ___.|a pleasant event remembered fondly|only a frightening dream during sleep|The speaker is evaluating an actual trip, not describing sleep.|The frustrating real journey selects the figurative experience sense.

19|The museum's carriage has wheels, seats and shafts for a horse to pull it.|Use the vehicle noun: In the historical display, a horse pulls a ___ carrying two people.|a compartment of a modern electric train in this scene|a stationary platform beside the track|Use the horse and shafts to choose the interpretation of the vehicle.|The explicit horse-drawn scene selects one of the bank's two vehicle meanings; the broader bank definition remains unchanged.

20|Numerous residents responded: the office received hundreds of letters.|Use the adjective meaning many: ___ visitors sent comments about the exhibition.|very few|exactly two|Use the scale of the response to judge quantity.|Hundreds of responses justify a large number rather than a small fixed count.

21|The council's scheme sets out a planned network of safer walking routes.|Use the noun for an organised plan: The committee discussed a ___ to improve access.|a random accident without planning|a single completed journey|Read the word as a structured public proposal, not necessarily a dishonest plot.|The written routes and aims make this an organised plan; no deception is stated.

22|At the meeting, the designer will propose adding a second entrance for consideration.|Use the base verb for putting an idea forward: The team will ___ a quieter route.|carry out without discussion|officially reject without consideration|Distinguish suggesting an option from approving or completing it.|The entrance is being put forward for discussion, so its construction has not been promised.

23|The revised timetable may resolve the clash between the two evening services.|Use the base verb for finding a solution: A new schedule could ___ the conflict.|describe without addressing|make the problem more severe|Ask whether the proposed change deals with the difficulty.|Removing the timetable clash would solve the identified problem.

24|The organisers hope to succeed in attracting enough volunteers to staff the event.|Use the base verb for achieving the intended result: With enough preparation, the team may ___.|fail to achieve the aim|stop before setting any aim|Compare the intended outcome with what the organisers hope to achieve.|Their desired result is sufficient volunteer support; success means reaching that aim.

25|A vocal advocate for accessible transport spoke repeatedly in favour of the proposal.|Use the two-word person phrase: Someone who publicly argues for the scheme is a ___.|someone who silently avoids taking a position|someone who consistently argues against the scheme|Notice both the public speaking and the support expressed.|Repeated public support makes the speaker an active advocate, not an objector.

26|In the fictional England-and-Wales setting, the client asks a solicitor to handle legal paperwork.|Use the legal-profession noun for this England-and-Wales context: The client consulted a ___ about the documents.|a person who repairs railway signals|a court witness with no professional legal role|Keep the specified jurisdiction and professional role in view.|The bank identifies a legal practitioner in England and Wales; the example does not claim the same professional system applies everywhere.

27|The evaluation considers social and economic advantages, including better access to services and more opportunities for local trade.|Use the four-word phrase: Improved services and stronger trade are discussed as ___.|costs affecting neither people nor business|only the colour and shape of buildings|The examples concern community life and economic activity together.|Access to services and opportunities for trade represent the two kinds of benefit; the example is not proof that every scheme delivers them.

28|The new footpath will link together the school grounds and the public garden.|Use the two-word verb phrase: A shared walkway can ___ the two entrances.|keep permanently separate|remove one place completely|Look for a connection between previously separate places.|The walkway connects the locations without making them the same place.

29|The archive records a plan to clear slums by removing poor-quality housing; the accompanying note asks what happened to displaced residents.|Use the historical two-word policy phrase: The document proposed to ___, while leaving residents' future housing unresolved.|improve every existing home without removal|guarantee an immediate benefit for every resident|Identify the physical action separately from whether its effects were fair or beneficial.|The phrase describes removal of poor-quality housing; it does not by itself establish rehousing, consent or a positive outcome.

31|The group meets in an inner-city centre close to the main commercial district.|Use the hyphenated adjective: The workshop is in an ___ neighbourhood near the centre.|located in a remote rural district|situated beyond every residential suburb|Use the location relative to the city centre.|The central location selects the geographical meaning rather than a judgment about the residents.

32|The newly constructed hall opened last week after the building work was completed.|Use the two-word phrase for recently built: The club moved into a ___ hall.|repaired many decades ago|not yet designed|Distinguish completion in the recent past from old age or future plans.|The recent completion and opening make the hall newly built.

35|The revised plan may gain support after the team addresses residents' concerns.|Use the two-word phrase for attracting backing: A clearer explanation could help the proposal ___.|lose all public backing|avoid being considered at all|Consider how approval from other people can grow.|Responding to concerns may attract backing; it does not guarantee unanimous approval.

36|The architect must submit a plan to the committee before it can review the design.|Use the three-word phrase: Before seeking approval, the designer will ___ to the board.|withdraw a design from consideration|complete construction without review|The action sends a proposal into an official review process.|The committee needs the plan presented formally before it can assess it.

37|The panel may reject the application because essential information is missing.|Use the base verb meaning refuse to accept: The committee could ___ the incomplete proposal.|approve without conditions|postpone work after granting permission|Focus on the decision about acceptance.|The missing information may lead to refusal; approval has not been granted.

38|The planned road closure will coincide with the annual street market on the same weekend.|Use the two-word phrase: The repairs will ___ the festival, with both happening on Saturday.|happen several years before|take place in a completely different season|Compare when the two events occur.|The shared weekend establishes simultaneous timing, not a causal connection.

39|The proposal describes a possible covered walkway and has not yet been approved.|Use the noun for a suggested plan: The board will discuss the designer's ___.|a confirmed record of completed work|a receipt proving payment|Distinguish an idea under consideration from a completed project.|The walkway is still a suggestion awaiting a decision.

40|After considering the changes, the committee voted to pass the proposal.|Use the base verb meaning officially approve: The committee may ___ the revised proposal.|refuse to approve the proposal|physically walk past the meeting room|Use the committee's decision-making sense of the verb.|In this context the vote gives official approval; it is not movement past an object.

41|The two small transport offices will merge into one organisation.|Use the base verb for combining into one body: The two teams plan to ___.|split into additional independent bodies|work nearby while remaining entirely separate|Compare the number of organisations before and after the change.|Two offices become one organisation, rather than simply sharing a location.

42|The partners will establish a new centre with a formal management structure.|Use the base verb for setting up formally: The group intends to ___ a training centre.|close an existing institution|visit briefly without organising anything|Focus on creating an organised institution.|The new centre and management structure indicate formal creation.

44|The museum hopes to raise funding for repairs through grants and donations.|Use the two-word phrase: The charity must ___ before it can pay for the project.|reduce the available project budget|spend money that has already been collected|Identify how money becomes available for a project.|Grants and donations provide project money; the phrase describes obtaining it.

45|The designer's radical proposal replaces the usual road layout with an entirely different arrangement.|Use the adjective for a major departure from convention: The architect suggested a ___ redesign.|closely following every established convention|making only an almost invisible adjustment|Compare the idea with the conventional approach.|Replacing the usual arrangement is a substantial departure, not a minor adjustment.

46|The town valued the evening service, not least because of its importance to shift workers.|Use the four-word phrase meaning especially because of: The route was welcomed, ___ its later departure time.|despite there being no relevant reason|only if every other reason is false|The phrase emphasises a strong reason without ruling out other reasons.|The shift-worker benefit is highlighted as an important reason, not necessarily the only one.

47|The reviewer was critical of the new timetable, pointing out several faults.|Use the adjective meaning expressing disapproval: The report was ___ of the poorly explained changes.|essential for a successful outcome in this sentence|entirely free from opinion|Use the listed faults to select the intended sense.|Pointing out faults expresses disapproval; the bank's target here is not the meaning essential.

48|The press reported on the opening: several newspapers and news outlets covered it.|Use the collective media noun: The opening attracted attention from the ___.|a machine used to flatten material in this context|a group consisting only of railway drivers|The examples identify organisations that report news.|The newspapers and news outlets identify the collective media sense.

49|An objector to the plan explained why she opposed the proposed closure.|Use the person noun: Someone who formally opposes a proposal is an ___.|a person giving unqualified support|a person who has expressed no position|Look at the person's stated opposition, not their occupation.|The objection concerns the closure; opposing the proposal makes the person an objector.

50|The authors argue that longer opening hours would improve access, giving reasons from their survey.|Use the base verb for presenting reasons: The researchers ___ that the service should be extended.|make a claim without any possible reasoning|quietly abandon a view without explaining it|Focus on making a case, not necessarily having an angry dispute.|The survey reasons support a reasoned position; an argument need not be a quarrel.

51|The historical drawing shows a damaged roof beginning to collapse after its supports failed.|Use the base verb meaning fall down suddenly: Without support, the damaged structure could ___.|remain perfectly upright and stable|be deliberately repainted|Consider what happens when a structure loses support.|The drawing depicts structural falling, not a change in decoration.

52|The visitors watched a banner hanging overhead, above the entrance.|Use the position word: A sign hung ___ as the group walked below it.|beneath the visitors' feet|inside a locked storage box|Locate the banner relative to the people looking up.|The banner is above the visitors, which selects the spatial sense.

53|Passing heavy traffic made the loose window shake rapidly.|Use the base verb for rapid repeated movement: Strong vibrations can make a loose panel ___.|remain completely motionless|change colour without moving|Track movement rather than appearance.|The vibration causes repeated movement of the window.

54|The fictional report warns that a toxic spill could poison the stream's wildlife.|Use the base verb for harming through a toxic substance: Such contamination can ___ aquatic animals.|provide harmless nourishment|improve water clarity without any harm|The report concerns a toxic effect on living things.|The stated toxicity and potential harm support this meaning; the task is a language example, not an instruction for handling chemicals.

56|Small delays persist even after the timetable has been adjusted.|Use the base verb for continuing despite efforts to stop something: The problem may ___ despite the changes.|stop as soon as it is noticed|occur once and never return|Look for continuation despite an attempted solution.|The adjustment has not ended the delays, so they continue.

57|A new ramp will enable wheelchair users to enter through the main doorway.|Use the base verb meaning make possible: Better access can ___ more people to attend.|prevent people from taking part|make no difference to what is possible|Focus on the possibility created by the change.|The ramp makes entry possible for users who previously faced a barrier.

58|The cooperative will invest some of its savings in new equipment.|Use the base verb for putting money into a project: The organisation plans to ___ in better facilities.|withdraw every resource from a project|observe a project without committing money|Identify the commitment of financial resources.|Using savings for equipment is a financial commitment to the project.

59|After several revisions, the team eventually agreed on a workable schedule.|Use the adverb meaning in the end after some time: After a long discussion, the members ___ reached agreement.|immediately before any discussion|repeatedly with no final outcome|Notice the final result after a period of effort.|Agreement comes after multiple revisions rather than at the start.

61|The diagram places the storage room beneath the main hall.|Use the preposition meaning underneath: The lower chamber lies ___ the entrance floor.|directly above|far beyond and unrelated to the site|Compare the vertical positions of the spaces.|The storage room occupies the lower position in the diagram.

63|The extra expense of a second entrance must be included in the budget.|Use the cost noun: The budget did not include the additional ___ of repairs.|income earned by selling tickets|the physical width of the doorway|Identify a cost that must be paid.|The entrance adds a cost to the budget, not revenue.

64|The archive records a decision to demolish the disused warehouse rather than repair it.|Use the base verb for deliberately destroying a building: The approved plan was to ___ the unsafe shed.|preserve every part without alteration|extend an existing room|Distinguish deliberate removal from repair or enlargement.|The decision concerns taking the structure down rather than restoring it.

65|The opening was originally scheduled for June, but the revised date is September.|Use the two-word phrase for the initial timing: The exhibition was ___ for spring before it was postponed.|planned only after the final revision|never assigned any date|Compare the first plan with the later change.|June belongs to the initial schedule; September is the revised date.

66|Construction of the footbridge took place before it opened to pedestrians.|Use the process noun: The building work continued during the final stage of ___.|the act of demolishing every structure|the daily use of a finished service|Separate making the structure from using it later.|The note describes the building process preceding public use.

67|The entrance is at street level, so visitors enter at the same height as the road.|Use the two-word height expression: The gallery doors are at ___ beside the pavement.|a floor far above the road|the deepest point of an underground tunnel|Compare the entrance height with the adjacent road surface.|The equal heights identify the level of the street.

68|The conservator demonstrated a technique for joining the model pieces neatly.|Use the method noun: The class practised a new ___ for assembling the display.|an accidental result with no method|a fixed amount of project money|Focus on the way an action is performed.|A demonstrated way of joining pieces is a method rather than a budget or outcome.

69|A museum caption calls the historical tunnelling method cut and cover: a trench was dug and later covered.|Use the three-word method name: The archive labels this trench-and-roof tunnelling approach ___.|boring a tunnel entirely without opening the surface|laying tracks only on an elevated viaduct|The method name follows the two stages described by the caption.|The caption explains the historical method through opening and covering a trench; it is not practical construction guidance.

70|The site drawing marks a trench as a long, narrow excavation in the ground.|Use the excavation noun: The diagram shows a long narrow ___ below the surface.|a tall tower built above the ground|a broad natural lake|Use the shape and the fact that material has been excavated.|The long narrow ground excavation distinguishes the feature from a tower or lake.

71|The reading room is temporarily closed and will reopen next week.|Use the adverb for a limited period: The entrance is ___ unavailable while repairs are completed.|permanently with no planned end|continuously since it first opened|The announced reopening sets a limit on duration.|The closure has a stated end, so it is not permanent.

72|In the display model, vertical columns hold up the roof above the central space.|Use the two-word verb phrase meaning support physically: The posts ___ the canopy.|delay the completion of an event in this sentence|decorate the roof without supporting it|Use the physical relationship between the columns and roof.|The columns support the roof; the target here is not the delay sense of the phrase.

73|The model labels a long wooden roof support as a timber beam.|Use the two-word structural noun phrase: A ___ supports the model roof.|a curved support made from bricks|a thin sheet of glass used as a window|Identify both the material and the supporting shape.|Wood and a long supporting member match this structural term.

74|The display shows a brick arch, with bricks arranged in a curved supporting shape.|Use the two-word structure phrase: The entrance drawing includes a curved ___ made of masonry units.|a straight wooden support|a flat layer of loose soil|Attend to the curve and the material together.|The combination of a curved form and bricks distinguishes the structure.

75|The diagram shows a layer of gravel lying above a separate thickness of sand.|Use the material-thickness noun: The drawing marks a thin ___ of soil above the stone.|a single point with no thickness|a route joining two distant towns|Look at one thickness within the stacked materials.|The gravel occupies a distinct thickness covering another material.

76|The club plans to rebuild the damaged pavilion after removing its ruined sections.|Use the base verb meaning build again: The group hopes to ___ the damaged shelter.|leave a damaged structure exactly as it is|construct something for the first time with no earlier structure|The task concerns a replacement for something that already existed.|The earlier damaged pavilion makes this an act of building again.

77|The new tram service began operation in April and has carried passengers since then.|Use the service-functioning noun: The line entered ___ after its final checks.|a medical procedure in this transport note|the planning of a service that never starts|Use the start of passenger service to select the sense.|Carrying passengers establishes that the transport service is functioning.

78|The railway extension adds two stations beyond the former end of the line.|Use the addition noun: The planned ___ will lengthen the existing railway.|the complete removal of every station|a shorter replacement with no added section|Compare the new section with the earlier railway.|The extra stations form an addition to the existing line.

79|The board may authorise the work after reviewing the application.|Use the base verb for giving official permission: The council can ___ the proposed change.|forbid an action after review|describe an action without permitting it|Focus on permission rather than physical performance of the work.|The board's role here is to permit the work, not to carry it out.

80|The museum's steam locomotive uses steam to power the train engine.|Use the two-word engine expression: The exhibit describes a train engine powered by steam as a ___.|a train engine powered only by an electric motor|a carriage with no means of propulsion|Identify what powers the engine.|The specified source of motive power distinguishes this engine from an electric one.

81|The archive diagram labels the equipment that heats water into steam as the boiler.|Use the equipment noun: The diagram identifies the water-heating vessel as the ___.|a device whose role is to generate electrical current|a vertical passage used only for air circulation|Focus on heating water rather than moving air or generating electricity.|The water-to-steam heating role selects this component in the diagram.

82|The library plans to introduce a new booking system next term.|Use the base verb for bringing something into use: The centre will ___ a new reservation service.|withdraw an existing system from use|keep an idea permanently unused|Consider the point at which a new system becomes available.|The proposed system is being brought into use rather than removed.

83|The updated model will be fitted with a small electric light during the display redesign.|Use the three-word installation phrase: The demonstration vehicle can ___ a new sensor.|have all its equipment removed|remain permanently unequipped|Focus on adding equipment to an existing object.|The phrase indicates that a component will be installed; the task does not give installation instructions.

85|The report describes fumes escaping from the old engine and notes their harmful gaseous nature.|Use the plural noun for strong harmful gases: The inspector reported ___ near the exhaust.|clean solid bricks used in construction|ordinary written comments in a report|Focus on what was released into the air.|The gaseous harmful emissions fit the target, unlike solid materials or text.

86|The diagram shows a ventilation shaft carrying air vertically between the tunnel and the surface.|Use the two-word air-passage expression: A vertical ___ links the enclosed space to the air above.|a horizontal rail carrying electrical current|a vessel that heats water into steam|Identify the passage's direction and air-circulation purpose.|A vertical route for circulating air is different from a power rail or boiler.

87|Traffic congestion left buses moving slowly among a large number of vehicles.|Use the traffic-condition noun: Heavy ___ increased journey times on the busy road.|a complete absence of road users|a timetable with unusually few scheduled services|Consider the crowding on the road rather than the service schedule.|The excessive volume of traffic explains the slow movement.

88|The walking route follows a circuit and returns visitors to their starting point.|Use the route noun: The marked ___ brings walkers back to the entrance.|a one-way route ending elsewhere|an isolated point with no route|Check whether the route closes back on its start.|Returning to the starting point makes the route a loop.

90|The small enclosed inspection room is described as a confined space in the fictional report.|Use the two-word space expression: The narrow enclosed chamber is a ___.|a broad open field|an unlimited outdoor area|Use the enclosure and limited room together.|The room is small and enclosed rather than open and extensive; this is a vocabulary description, not an entry-safety assessment.

91|The service is reliable: it consistently arrives at the advertised time.|Use the adjective meaning dependable: Travellers value a ___ connection that works as expected.|frequently failing without warning|unable to follow any consistent pattern|Consider whether users can depend on the service.|Consistent performance supports dependability rather than unpredictability.

92|The display's electric motor turns the small wheel using electrical energy.|Use the two-word device expression: A device driven by electricity turns the model; it is an ___.|an engine driven by steam alone|a passive seat with no moving mechanism|Identify the energy source and the device producing movement.|Electrical energy drives the motor; the term is not a steam engine or passive object.

93|The ferry provides a means of crossing the river when the bridge is closed.|Use the two-word method phrase: A shared path offers a ___ reaching the station on foot.|a reason for avoiding every journey|the final destination rather than a way to reach it|Focus on how an activity can be done.|The ferry is a way to cross, not the reason for the journey or its destination.

94|The model uses a belt to transfer power from the motor to the wheel.|Use the two-word energy phrase: The connection can ___ from the drive unit to the moving part.|store all energy without passing it on|measure distance without moving energy|Follow energy from one device to another.|The belt conveys energy between components rather than merely storing it.

96|The archive describes a deep-level electric railway running far below the streets on electrical power.|Use the three-word rail expression: An electrically powered line far below ground is a ___.|a horse-drawn line operating on the street|a steam railway running on an elevated bridge|Combine the depth of the line with its power source.|Both the underground depth and electrical power are necessary to select this description.

97|The exhibition will be made up of six sections, each covering a different topic.|Use the four-word composition phrase: The display will ___ three linked panels.|be positioned entirely outside|be removed before anyone sees it|Identify the relationship between a whole and its components.|The sections are the parts composing the exhibition.

98|The passage is narrow, leaving little width between its two walls.|Use the width adjective: The corridor is ___ rather than wide.|very wide|unusually tall but with no information about width|Judge the distance from one side to the other.|The close walls indicate limited width, not a measurement of height.

100|The successful completion of the new control system was described as a technical achievement.|Use the two-word accomplishment phrase: Developing a working new transport system was a ___.|a technological failure with no successful result|a routine financial loss unrelated to technology|Connect the successful result with technological work.|A functioning new system is presented as a technological accomplishment.

101|The café must earn more than its costs if it is to make a profit.|Use the three-word financial phrase: When income exceeds expenses, the business can ___.|spend more than it earns|receive no income at all|Compare income with the amount spent.|Earnings above costs produce a surplus rather than a loss.

102|The new booking arrangements are in place and are already being used by staff.|Use the two-word phrase for established and functioning: The revised system is now ___.|still only an unimplemented suggestion|removed from service permanently|Notice that the arrangements have begun working.|Actual staff use shows that the arrangements are established, not merely proposed.

103|The hall opened in May; soon afterwards, evening classes began there.|Use the two-word time phrase: The centre opened, and ___ the first workshop took place.|many years before the opening|at an unspecified time with no relation to the opening|Use the short interval and the order of the events.|The classes followed the opening after a short time rather than preceding it.
